title: "Research"
subtitle: "Public opinion, behaviour and policy in climate and energy challenges"
description: "Research on public opinion, political psychology, energy transitions, climate risk, fairness, policy processes and place-based decision-making."
---

My research brings together **public policy, political psychology, behavioural science and environmental social science** to understand how people and communities respond to climate and energy challenges. Across this work, I examine both what people want governments and institutions to do—through public opinion, policy preferences and technology acceptance—and what people themselves do, or are willing to do, through mitigation, adaptation, preparedness and other behavioural responses.

I am also developing a complementary strand of research on how public and community priorities can inform evidence generation, policy design and decision-making, particularly where climate and energy transitions create uneven costs, benefits and opportunities across places and groups.

## Research themes

::: {.card-grid}
::: {.research-card}
<div class="card-icon">A</div>

### Public Opinion, Political Psychology & Environmental Policy

I examine how people form opinions and preferences about environmental, climate and energy policy. This research focuses on how values, political and social identities, beliefs, knowledge, information, social norms and issue priorities shape public attitudes, policy preferences and behavioural responses.
:::

::: {.research-card}
<div class="card-icon">B</div>

### Energy Transitions, Public Acceptance & Fairness

I study how people and communities evaluate low-carbon technologies, infrastructure and energy developments. My work examines how perceived risks and benefits, project attributes, narratives and policy rationales shape public acceptance and support, as well as how people evaluate community benefits, trade-offs and the distribution of costs and benefits.
:::

::: {.research-card}
<div class="card-icon">C</div>

### Climate Risk, Extreme Weather & Resilience

I investigate how people understand and respond to environmental hazards and extreme weather. This research examines how lived experience, perceived harm, prior beliefs, political orientations, information and social norms shape preparedness, community helping, climate action and support for mitigation and adaptation policies.
:::

::: {.research-card}
<div class="card-icon">D</div>

### Policy Processes, Evidence & Place-Based Transitions

My emerging research examines how evidence, institutions and public and community priorities shape climate and energy decision-making. I am particularly interested in what evidence decision-makers and communities need, how local priorities and fairness concerns can inform policy appraisal, and when locally grounded evidence changes assessments of costs, benefits and distributional impacts.
:::
:::

## Ocean-REFuel <span class="project-date">2024–present</span> {#ocean-refuel}

**University of Bath · EPSRC-funded interdisciplinary programme**

Ocean-REFuel investigates the potential to convert ocean renewable energy into liquid and gaseous zero-carbon fuels, including hydrogen and ammonia, and brings together researchers in engineering, economics, psychology and policy studies from several UK universities. Within this broader programme, my work focuses on the **social, psychological and policy dimensions of future energy systems**: public attitudes and acceptance, perceived risks and benefits, policy rationales, and the ways people and communities evaluate proposed energy developments. This work draws on **nationwide survey experiments** and **deliberative workshops** to examine both national public responses and place-based transition processes.

[Ocean-REFuel project website](https://www.oceanrefuel.ac.uk/) · [University of Bath project page](https://researchportal.bath.ac.uk/en/projects/ocean-refuel-ocean-renewable-energy-fuels-2/)

## Methods

My research combines **quantitative, experimental, qualitative and mixed-method approaches**. I am especially interested in designs that can identify how people make trade-offs, how attitudes are structured, and how evidence can inform policy design and public engagement.

::: {.method-grid}
::: {.method-card}
### Surveys & experiments
Survey design and implementation · choice-based conjoint experiments · survey experiments · panel and repeated cross-sectional designs
:::
::: {.method-card}
### Statistical modelling
Structural equation modelling · conjoint analysis . path analysis · factor and cluster analysis · regression models · fixed-, random- and mixed-effects models
:::
::: {.method-card}
### Qualitative & mixed methods
Interviews · focus groups · deliberative workshops · ethnography . participatory approaches · interpretative qualitative methods
:::
::: {.method-card}
### Additional training in causal and programme-evaluation methods
Randomised controlled trials · instrumental variables · regression discontinuity · difference-in-differences
:::
:::

<div class="skill-strip"><strong>Software:</strong> Stata · SPSS · AMOS · Excel · R · Python · NVivo</div>

## Earlier research

Before specialising in environmental and energy policy, my research addressed a broader range of questions in political science and public policy, including political trust, governance, policing, representation, political development and international affairs, with much of this work focused on Pakistan.
